paper_profile.title: Remote Memory Calls
paper_profile.abstract: In this paper we propose an extension to RDMA, called Remote Memory Calls (RMCs), that allows applications to install a customized set of 1-sided RDMA operations. We then explain how RMCs can be implemented on the forthcoming generation of SmartNICs and discuss the resulting tradeoffs between RMCs, 1-sided RDMA operations, and 2-sided RDMA operations.
paper_profile.research_problem: The paper addresses the gap between the narrow set of 1-sided RDMA operations implemented in NIC hardware and the broader, more complex memory access patterns required by real distributed applications, which currently forces applications to either use inflexible 1-sided operations or CPU-expensive 2-sided operations.
methods: Modeling of latencies for linked list scan and remote buffer hashing workloads
Microbenchmark comparing RDMA read throughput between NIC-Host and Host-Host
main_contributions: Proposes Remote Memory Calls (RMCs), an extension to RDMA that allows applications to install customized 1-sided RDMA operations
Explains how RMCs can be implemented on forthcoming CPU-based SmartNICs
Provides a feasibility analysis of implementing RMCs on SmartNICs, focusing on Mellanox Bluefield-1
Discusses tradeoffs between RMCs, 1-sided RDMA operations, and 2-sided RDMA operations
Demonstrates benefits of RMCs through modeling of linked list scanning and remote buffer hashing workloads
claimed_innovations: RMCs as a specialization of software RPCs to memory-oriented remote operations
RMCs as an abstraction that can be executed at the server SmartNIC, server CPU, client SmartNIC, or client CPU, enabling runtime decisions about remote memory access
Use of compiler-assisted isolation, eBPF-style verification, and semantically-constrained programming languages to address implementation challenges
experimental_results: For 1KB reads, Host-Host achieves 10.2M reads/s while NIC-Host achieves 9.6M reads/s (94% of Host-Host)
For 128B reads, Host-Host achieves 19.4M reads/s while NIC-Host achieves 9.5M reads/s (49% of Host-Host)
In Bluefield-1, the round-trip time of 1-sided RDMA reads from another host is lower (2.7µs) than the RTT from the BF1 CPU (3.1µs) to its host memory
Both DMA-based RMC results show better latency relative to 1-sided when scanning lists with 4 or more nodes, with the latency gap increasing with list length
RMCs allow a constant amount of data transfer (24 bytes request, 8 bytes result) for linked list scans, while 1-sided operations transfer data proportional to list length
For hashing workloads, RMCs on BF1 can provide comparable latency to 1-sided operations once access size grows sufficiently
RMCs reduce the amount of bulk data transferred over the network fabric, reducing congestion
limitations: RMCs implemented on today's SmartNICs (BF1) would decrease network load but would not decrease delays compared to 1-sided operations
Host memory access latency, especially for small memory reads, is the main impediment to achieving the RMC vision on current hardware
Limited NIC resources will restrict the size (number of instructions) and runtime of RMCs
A complete RMC API specification and concrete programming model are left for future work
paper_profile.summary: This paper proposes Remote Memory Calls (RMCs), an extension to RDMA that allows applications to install customized 1-sided RDMA operations. RMCs are memory-oriented software procedures registered and invoked by a client and executed by a remote server's RDMA NIC CPUs, supporting operations such as reading/writing host memory, atomics, conditional branching, monitoring writes, and basic computation. The paper argues that forthcoming CPU-based SmartNICs (focusing on Mellanox Bluefield-1) will have the hardware capabilities to efficiently support RMCs, and provides a feasibility analysis covering PCIe bandwidth, NIC-to-host memory access latency, and RMC execution rate. The authors identify host memory access latency, especially for small reads, as the main current impediment, but project that faster CPUs, new IO busses, and software improvements will resolve this. They model two workloads (linked list scanning and remote buffer hashing) comparing RMCs to 1-sided RDMA, finding that RMCs reduce network load and congestion but on current BF1 hardware do not reduce latency; however, idealized future SmartNICs would yield decreased latency for workloads with repeated host memory accesses. The paper also discusses implementation challenges including low-cost memory isolation, preemption and scheduling, and programming language design, and analyzes tradeoffs between RMCs, 1-sided, and 2-sided operations, arguing that RMCs as an abstraction enable runtime decisions about remote memory access location.
